docs.title: Workflow
docs.text:
mpctrano sits downstream of Trano. The building description (house.yaml) stays the single source of truth: Trano renders it into Modelica models with its FastModel library, mpctrano calibrates them on monitoring data, estimates their state and controls the systems of the building.

 house.yaml ──trano (FastModelMPC)──▶ building_mpc ──rumoca──▶ CasADi ODE  xdot = f(t, x, u, p)
            ──trano (FastModel)─────▶ the same building with the controllers of the YAML (rule-based reference)

docs.title: 1. Model
docs.text:
from mpctrano import FastModel

model = FastModel.from_yaml("house.yaml")                       # calls Trano (FastModelMPC library)
model = FastModel.from_file("house.mo")                         # or the package of `trano create-model house.yaml FastModelMPC`
closed_loop = FastModel.from_yaml("house.yaml", library="FastModel")  # the controllers of the YAML

The FastModelMPC model is close to the Buildings library: layered walls and floors, windows with the angular optics of their glazing, convection and long-wave exchanges in the room, infiltration, the hydronic circuits of the YAML (radiators, valves, mixing valves, pumps, boilers, air-to-water heat pumps and their buffer), ventilation units with heat recovery and PV arrays. The controls of the systems are inputs. FastModel reads everything from the Modelica model:

  • control_names - the inputs with a min and a max: valve positions, mixing valves, boiler part load ratio or heat pump speed (between 0 and 1), the heat of ideal emitters [W];
  • disturbance_names - the weather channels (weather_inputs.TDryBul, .TBlaSky, .winSpe, .winDir, .HDirNor, .HDifHor, .HGloHor) and the internal gains per floor area of each occupancy model (<occupancy>_gai.QRad, .QCon);
  • comfort_states - the air temperature of each zone (<zone>.TAir);
  • meters - the energy the systems drew or produced since the start, states in kWh: EFue (fuel), EEle (electricity of a heat pump), EFan (fans), EPro (PV);
  • simulate(x0, controls, disturbances, dt, start_time) - CVODES simulation, controls held over each step; the model depends on the time of the year (the solar position is computed inside it);
  • with_parameters({...}), select_parameters(patterns), write(directory).

The model is nonlinear and stiff (water nodes): the optimisation problems collocate it on Radau points (trano_optimization), which keeps them stable whatever the step. rumoca does not report the unit of array states (wall layers, radiator water): FastModel restores the kelvin on them so that the collocation scales and bounds them as temperatures.

The variables are named after the elements of the YAML (space_001.TAir, boiler_001.EEle, externalwall_0.G[1]): FastModel.from_yaml generates the model without the containers Trano groups the elements in since 0.57 (network.model(include_container=False)), and FastModel.from_file strips their prefixes (envelope1., production1., ...) from a containerised model, as written by trano create-model. Both give the same model; tests/test_trano_contract.py checks it, with the translation of Trano's models by rumoca, against the installed Trano.

The CasADi export of these models needs rumoca 0.10.3 (rumoca main up to commit c74cddf); uv sync builds it from source, see the installation section of the README. The collocation, the moving horizon estimation and the CasADi model come from trano-optimization (formerly trano.optimization).

docs.title: 2. Disturbances
docs.text: WeatherForecaster.from_model(model) reads the TMY3 .mos weather file of the runnable model (a file of the same name next to the YAML) and the occupancy schedules of the YAML: the weather channels at the middle of each step, the black-body sky temperature computed as the Buildings weather reader does (from the dew point and the opaque sky cover), and the radiant and convective gains of each occupancy model. ForecastNoise adds lead-time dependent errors to the temperatures, the irradiance and the gains; DataForecaster replays recorded disturbances.

docs.title: 4. Closed loop, scenarios and the rule-based reference
docs.text:
run_closed_loop(controller, estimator, plant, forecaster, steps) runs the cycle measure → correct → forecast → solve → apply → predict against a ModelPlant (a FastModel playing the real building, with sensor noise) and returns a ClosedLoopResult with the trajectories and the ControlMetrics, read from the meters of the plant: fuel and electricity bought and sold, cost at the price of each carrier, capacity charge, comfort violation in K·h, peak electric power, share of the energy bought below the median price.

run_rule_based(closed_loop, forecaster, start, steps, dt, comfort, tariff) simulates the closed-loop FastModel of the same YAML, with the controllers it describes (thermostats on the valves, the boiler or heat pump holding its supply temperature, the mixing valve its set point), costed and assessed the same way: the reference the MPC is compared with.

Scenario bundles a tariff, a comfort specification, the MPC settings, the forecast noise and the estimator; run_scenario, run_scenario_rule_based and Project.run / Project.run_rule_based execute it; compare puts several runs side by side.

The executed tutorial notebooks are in the Tutorials section of this site; their source is in tutorials/, and each one opens in Google Colab with its Open in Colab badge (06_your_building to edit the building itself).

docs.title: Calibration
docs.text:
A FastModel has hundreds of parameters, most of them settled by the YAML (areas, orientations, the optical fits of the glazing) or not identifiable from a few air temperatures. Calibrator adjusts groups of parameters instead, each by one decision variable:

Group Parameters Mode, range envelope_conductance conductances of the wall, floor and roof layers (G[i]), of the glazing gaps and frames factor 0.25-4 envelope_capacity capacities of the layers (C[i]) and of the panes factor 0.25-4 air_capacity the heat capacity factor of the air of each zone (mSenFac, furniture) factor 1-10 infiltration the air changes per hour of each zone (ACH, 0 in Trano) value 0-3 1/h boiler_efficiency the nominal efficiency of the boilers (from the fuel meter) factor 0.7-1.1

OPTIONAL_GROUPS adds the solar transmittance of the windows and the capacity of the radiators, which the air temperatures hardly identify on their own. A ParameterGroup is a set of regular expressions on the parameter names, a mode (scale: the Trano values times a common factor; value: one common value) and bounds; only the parameters the equations depend on are adjusted (the conductances and capacities trano computed from the layers, not the layer data). The heat output of the radiators and the performance maps of the heat pumps are settled when rumoca translates the model and cannot be calibrated.

from mpctrano import Calibrator, CalibrationSettings

calibrator = Calibrator(model, CalibrationSettings(temperature_std=0.1, meter_std=0.05))
calibrated, result = calibrator.fit(training, validation)
result.factors       # the value of each group
result.metrics()     # RMSE and MAE of the air temperatures, training and validation, before and after

The problem is solved with IPOPT by one of two methods (CalibrationSettings.method, auto by default):

  • collocation, for a model with control inputs: the Radau collocation of the model over the whole period, the parameters symbolic. The states of every step are decision variables bound by the dynamics, so that a long period and poor initial parameters stay well conditioned, and the unmeasured states (walls, water) are free at the start.
  • shooting, for a closed-loop model (the controllers of the YAML inside, no control input): the groups are the only decision variables; the model is simulated with CVODES inside the objective from the state its own controllers reach before the data (spin_up), and IPOPT gets the gradient from the adjoint sensitivities of the integrator, with a quasi-Newton (L-BFGS) Hessian. The thermostats and hysteresis of such a model make its collocated dynamics non-smooth (IPOPT then crawls without converging), where a simulation follows them in a second.

The objective weighs the errors of the air temperatures (temperature_std), of the energy metered over each step (meter_std) and the deviation of each group from the Trano value (prior_std, regularization). The validation period is simulated from where the training ends.

On the boiler house of the tests, with the conductances x1.3, the capacities x0.8, the air capacity x3, 0.5 air changes per hour and the boiler efficiency x0.9, four days recover x1.35, x0.80, x2.74, 0.47 and x0.904 in about 30 s; the air temperature error falls from 4.5 K to 0.06 K (0.07 K on two validation days). With a single day, the conductances and the infiltration trade with each other: both are losses to the outdoor air.

evaluate(model, data, x0) and simulate_fit(model, data, x0) give the open-loop fit of any model; Project.save() writes the calibration to <stem>.calibration.json and Project.load_calibrated() reads it back.

docs.title: Smoothing the controllers
docs.text:
The thermostats, hysteresis and limiters of a Trano FastModel are steep smooth switches (trano >= 0.59 exposes their widths dU, dY, dMax, dT, dtSet and the switching time tau as parameters). CVODES follows them, but each switch that moves by a sample under a parameter change makes the objective jumpy at the 0.1 % scale, which is what forces the wide finite differences of the shooting method. FastModel.smooth_controllers(width_factor=5.0, switching_time=600.0) returns a copy whose transitions are five times wider and whose hysteresis switches over ten minutes; calibrate that copy and apply the factors to the sharp model.

On the single-zone house of the tests (truth k = 0.06 W/(m.K), known infiltration, three days of data with 0.1 K of noise, four cores):

Controllers Smoothed truth vs sharp data Shooting Collocation sharp (trano) 0.09 K (the noise) 211 s, 17 it, k = 0.0594 no convergence x1, 600 s 0.23 K 22 s, 8 it, k = 0.0531 no convergence x5, 600 s 0.14 K 14 s, 7 it, k = 0.0594 no convergence x10, 600 s 0.27 K 11 s, 7 it, k = 0.0448 72 s, 48 it, k = 0.0448 x20, 600 s 0.42 K 9 s, 5 it, k = 0.025 130 s, 37 it, k = 0.025 (the bound)

The switching time is what smooths the objective (the sharp model and x1 differ only by it); the width is what costs fidelity, and from x10 on it smears the thermostat band enough to bias the conductances low. Collocation converges only on controllers too smooth to be faithful, so the shooting method on the x5, 600 s copy is the setting to use.

docs.title: Parameters declared in the YAML
docs.text:
The YAML of the building can declare the parameters to calibrate itself, so that it stays the single source of truth: a numeric field written as a mapping with its nominal value and its bounds, instead of the bare number Trano expects.

material:
  - id: ROCKWOOL:CAL
    thermal_conductivity: {value: 0.04, parameter: true, min: 0.025, max: 0.08}
constructions:
  - id: CAVITYWALL:CAL
    layers:
      - material: ROCKWOOL:CAL
        thickness: {value: 0.1, parameter: true, min: 0.04, max: 0.2}
spaces:
  - id: SPACE:001
    variant: infiltration
    parameters:
      ach: {value: 0.3, parameter: true, min: 0.05, max: 1.5}

CalibrationSpec reads the file, addresses the fields by path (the convention of trano.runtime: material[ROCKWOOL:CAL].thermal_conductivity, spaces[SPACE:001].parameters.ach) and writes the flat copy Trano reads. Which parameters of the CasADi model a field moves is measured, not assumed: the model is regenerated with the field raised by 20 % and the exponent of every parameter that moved is read (a conductivity moves the conductances of its layers with the exponent 1, a thickness moves them with -1 and the node capacities with a small exponent). The calibration then adjusts the field within its bounds and every dependent parameter with it (YamlGroup); the factors of fields that move the same parameter compound (a conductivity and a thickness both move the conductance of the insulation layer).

from mpctrano import CalibrationSettings, CalibrationSpec, Calibrator, generate_closed_loop_data, spin_up

spec = CalibrationSpec.from_yaml("house.yaml")
model = spec.model("FastModel")                     # the closed loop: the controllers of the YAML, no control input
groups = spec.groups(model, "FastModel")            # one regeneration per declared field
calibrated, result = Calibrator(model, CalibrationSettings(groups=groups)).fit(data)
result.factors                                      # {"material[ROCKWOOL:CAL].thermal_conductivity": 0.058, ...}

The data of a closed-loop model holds no control: the disturbances, the measured air temperatures and the meter readings are enough, as a monitoring system that logs the sensors and the meters but not the valves records. generate_closed_loop_data records such data on a true building, for instance the YAML with other values of its parameters (spec.model("FastModel", {"...ach": 0.6})), with sensor and meter noise, which is how the tests check that the calibration recovers them.

Trano's own tools do not read the annotations (its validation rejects unknown keys); mpctrano writes the flat copy before calling it. A value / parameter / min / max convention in Trano's schema would make the annotated file valid everywhere.

docs.title: Monitoring data
docs.text:
MonitoringData wraps a regularly sampled, time-indexed DataFrame whose columns are named after the variables of the FastModel:

Column Unit Role time timestamp (first column of the CSV by default) <zone>.TAir K/°C measured air temperature of a zone (at least one zone) valve_001_y.y, boiler_001_y.y, ... - the controls applied, held from each sample to the next boiler_001.EEle, boiler_001.EFue, ... kWh readings of the energy meters, cumulative (optional) weather_inputs.TDryBul, ... K, W/m², m/s, rad the weather channels (optional) occupancy_1_gai.QCon, .QRad W/m² internal gains per floor area (optional; occupancy_1.gai.* before Trano 0.57) 
from mpctrano import MonitoringData

data = MonitoringData.from_csv("monitoring.csv", temperature_unit="C", rename={"Living room": "space_001.TAir"})
report = data.validate(model)              # measured zones, controls, meters, missing columns, gaps
data = data.fill_disturbances(model, forecaster)  # weather file and occupancy schedules for the rest
training, validation = data.split(fraction=0.75)  # the validation starts where the training ends

resample(dt) averages the data on another period, window(start, end) cuts a period, to_csv(path, temperature_unit="C") writes it back.

Without a building at hand, Project.synthetic_data() (or generate_monitoring_data) records data on a copy of the model with its parameter groups at random values (perturb), operated by a thermostat with a random set point that excites the dynamics: the controls, the measured air temperatures with sensor noise, the meter readings and the disturbances.

docs.title: State estimation
docs.text:
The MPC needs the full state of the FastModel (the air, the layers of the walls, the panes, the radiator and buffer water) at the start of each horizon, but only the zone air temperatures are measured. Every estimator follows the cycle correct with the measurement of the step → use the state → predict with the inputs applied during the step (StateEstimator).

MovingHorizonEstimator(model, dt, start, settings=EstimatorSettings(window=12)) keeps the inputs applied and the measurements of the last window steps and, at each correct, finds the trajectory of the model closest to them with the moving horizon estimation of trano_optimization (Radau collocation, IPOPT): the measured air temperatures (measurement_noise), the model errors over each step (process_noise) and the deviation of the first state of the window from its prior (arrival_noise) are weighted by their standard deviations. When the window slides, the estimate of its second state becomes the prior of the next window; when an estimation fails, the prior is propagated over the step instead. Each estimation takes a fraction of a second.

On the boiler house of the tests started 2 K colder than the estimator assumes, the mean error over its 26 temperature states falls from 1.9 K to 0.05 K within a day, where the uncorrected model keeps 0.84 K; the closed-loop MPC with estimation costs the same as with the true state.

PerfectEstimator(plant) returns the true state of a simulated plant, to study the controller alone.

docs.title: Model predictive control, tariffs and flexibility
Optimisation problem
docs.text:
At every step, from the estimated state x0, the time t0 and the forecasts over N steps of dt seconds, ModelPredictiveController solves with IPOPT:

min   Σ_k (π_k b_k − π^in_k (b_k − e_k) + π^fuel_k f_k)    energy cost [EUR], prices in EUR/kWh
    + c_cap · P_peak / 1000                                 capacity charge [EUR/kW] on the peak electric power
    + Σ_k (w₁ (s⁻ + s⁺) + w₂ (s⁻² + s⁺²)) · dt / 3600       comfort violations [K·h]
    + w_lim · Σ_k s_lim,k · dt / 3.6e6                      electricity above a demand response power limit
    + w_move · Σ_k |v_k − v_{k−1}|² + w_effort · Σ_k |v_k|²   moves and effort of the controls (scaled to [0, 1])
s.t.  the FastModel collocated on Radau IIA points in each step
      the bounds of each control (0-1 for the valves, the heat pump speed and the boiler load)
      T_lower,k − s⁻_k ≤ T_zone,k+1 ≤ T_upper,k + s⁺_k        soft comfort band on every zone
      P_k ≤ limit_k + s_lim,k,     P_k ≤ P_peak                electric power bought from the grid

e_k is the net electricity of step k [kWh], read from the meters of the model (the electricity of the heat pumps and fans, the heat of the ideal emitters, minus the PV production), b_k its smooth positive part (bought, the rest is sold at the feed-in price), f_k the fuel the boilers drew and P_k = b_k / dt the electric power. Since the energy comes from the meters, the efficiency of the systems is part of the plan: the COP of a heat pump is better in the mild afternoon than in the cold night, the efficiency of a boiler depends on its load and its water temperature.

MPCSettings holds the horizon, the time step, the penalties, fuel_price and feed_in_price (the tariff price when not given) and the IPOPT options. The problem is built once (casadi.Opti with the time, the forecasts, the prices and the bounds as parameters) and every solve() updates them and warm starts IPOPT from a CVODES simulation of the previous plan shifted by one step, with a small initial barrier parameter (warm_mu_init), which halves the iterations of the receding-horizon solves. If IPOPT does not converge the last iterate is returned with success=False (the closed loop keeps running and counts the failures), and the next solve starts cold.

Comfort bounds apply at the end of each step (the occupied band starting at 7h constrains the temperature reached at 7h); prices apply to the energy of the step. controller.energy gives the electricity bought and net, the fuel and the electric power of each step of the last plan.

On the heat pump house of the tests (27 states), a 24-hour plan with hourly steps solves in 5 to 20 s; the six-zone heat pump house of the Trano test suite (111 states) takes over a minute.

docs.title: Tariffs
docs.text:
Tariff Description FlatTariff one price TimeOfUseTariff peak / off-peak hours, weekends off-peak unless weekend_peak DynamicTariff a price series (from_csv, synthetic_day_ahead), held between samples DemandResponseTariff any tariff + DemandResponseEvents: price multiplier and/or power cap

The tariffs price the electricity; the fuel has its own price (MPCSettings.fuel_price). Every tariff can carry a capacity_charge [EUR/kW] on the peak electric power of the horizon. A DemandResponseEvent power cap applies to the electric power bought from the grid; it is a soft constraint with a high penalty (power_limit_penalty): it is respected unless comfort would collapse.

docs.title: Comfort
docs.text: ComfortSchedule defines occupied/unoccupied bands in °C with the occupied hours; ComfortSpec assigns a schedule per zone (default otherwise) and map("widen", delta) or map("constant") transforms all of them.

docs.title: Flexibility
docs.text:
The flexibility of a building is what the thermal mass and the buffers allow between the bounds: with a cheap night the controller pre-heats and lets the temperature float during the expensive hours; with a capacity charge it spreads the morning boost; during a demand response event it sheds load. The comfort band is the lever: wide_comfort_band in the scenario catalogue raises its upper bound by 2 K.

Costs are only comparable under the same tariff. value_of_flexibility(model, scenario) runs the scenario twice, with the price-aware MPC and with a price-agnostic one (flat price, same comfort band and model), costs both runs with the tariff of the scenario and reports the saving, the energy shifted and the share of energy bought at low prices.

The reference of a building is its own control: run_rule_based (or Project.run_rule_based) simulates the controllers of the YAML on the same building. On the boiler house of the tests, over a January day with the band of its thermostat, the MPC costs 12 % less than the controllers of the YAML under a flat and under a time-of-use tariff, with almost no discomfort (0.05 K·h against 3.7 K·h, the warm-up of the thermostat), and buys 30 % of its energy off-peak against 10 %.

The controller can only exploit the storage it believes in: with the uncalibrated Trano parameters against a different real building, the pre-heating is mis-sized and the comfort band is missed (tutorial 5 shows it). Calibrate before trusting the price response.

compare(runs, baseline="flat") puts several runs side by side (same tariff for the costs to be comparable):

  • total_cost, cost_saving_pct - energy plus capacity cost and the saving against the baseline,
  • energy_kwh, energy_change_pct - pre-heating costs some extra energy,
  • shifted_energy_kwh - energy moved in time against the baseline (half of the L1 distance of the hourly profiles),
  • low_price_share, mean_price - share of the energy bought below the median price, average price paid,
  • comfort_violation_kh, max_violation, peak_power_kw.

price_response(run) gives the energy bought at each price level.

docs.title: Cooling with ideal emitters
docs.text:
The ideal emitter of a zone (radiator of variant ideal in the YAML) is a heat flow input of the FastModelMPC model, which Trano bounds to heating (min=0). FastModel.with_control_bounds gives it a negative lower bound: the same equations cool the zone. The controller costs its heat at MPCSettings.heat_cop and its cooling at MPCSettings.cooling_eer (electricity per unit of heat or cooling); the closed loop meters it alike.

office = FastModel.from_yaml("office.yaml").with_control_bounds({"emitter_001_Q.Q_flow": (-12000.0, None)})
settings = MPCSettings(horizon=24, heat_cop=3.5, cooling_eer=3.0)

docs.title: Electrical storages at the meter
docs.text:
A stationary battery and an electric vehicle are optimised in the balance of the meter next to the thermal storage of the building (mpctrano.storage): linear state-of-charge models with a round-trip efficiency and power bounds; the vehicle charges while plugged in (arrival_hour to departure_hour), leaves with at least departure_energy_kwh (soft, at missing_energy_price) and comes back driven_kwh lower. The controller carries their state from one solve to the next (ModelPredictiveController.advance, called by the closed loop) and reports the plan in MPCSolution.storage.

settings = MPCSettings(
    horizon=24,
    batteries=(Battery(capacity_kwh=8, max_charge_w=3000, max_discharge_w=3000),),
    vehicles=(ElectricVehicle(capacity_kwh=50, max_charge_w=7400, arrival_hour=18, departure_hour=7, driven_kwh=12),),
)

The energy stored in a battery at the end of the horizon is valued at the mean price of the horizon, so that the controller does not empty it before the end.

docs.title: Tutorials
docs.text:
Hands-on notebooks on the energy flexibility of buildings with economic model predictive control, from a Trano YAML description to flexibility indicators. The pages of this section are the executed notebooks of tutorials/: the figures are interactive, the widgets of the live sections are not: open the notebook in Google Colab with its Open in Colab badge (the first cell installs everything), or in JupyterLab after the installation of the tutorials README. 06_your_building is the notebook to edit: the building is a YAML cell.

The closed-loop runs the notebooks read come from a committed cache (tutorials/cache/), built by make cache; the references are listed in tutorials/references.md and the plan of the series in tutorials/PLAN.md.

docs.text:
Learning objectives

  • confirm that the toolchain of the tutorials is installed: trano (YAML to Modelica), rumoca (Modelica to CasADi, the commit uv sync builds), trano-optimization (collocation), casadi with IPOPT, mpctrano;
  • generate a first CasADi model from a Trano YAML with the FastModelMPC library and plan its heating.

Run this notebook first; every other tutorial assumes it passes. In continuous integration the notebooks run with MPCTRANO_QUICK=1 (shorter periods), see tutorials/README.md.

docs.title: From a Trano YAML to a CasADi model¶
docs.text: FastModel.from_yaml runs the whole chain: Trano renders the FastModelMPC Modelica model of the building (building_mpc: the walls, the windows, the heat pump, its buffer, the mixing valve and the radiator, the controls of the systems as inputs), rumoca translates it into the CasADi ODE xdot = f(t, x, u, p), and the roles of the variables are read from the Modelica model.

docs.title: IPOPT is available¶
docs.text: A plan of the MPC on the model confirms that CasADi can call IPOPT (with SPRAL when CasADi ships it).

docs.title: 01 - A house with a heat pump: the reference implementation¶
docs.text:
Learning objectives

  1. Follow the pipeline from the Trano YAML to the CasADi model: what the FastModel of a house contains, which inputs the controller decides and which ones it has to forecast, where the energy is metered.
  2. Read an economic MPC plan: how the comfort band, the price signal and the horizon shape the heating of a heat pump house with a buffer tank and a radiator.
  3. Run the closed loop against a building that is not the control model (perturbed envelope, noisy sensors) and compare it with the controllers written in the YAML.
  4. See why state estimation matters: the controller needs the walls, the water and the buffer, it measures the air temperature only.

Everything here calls the library; the closed loops come from tutorials/cache/house/ (uv run python tutorials/scripts/build_cache.py house). The plan widget solves live.

Runtimes (hourly steps, this container): Trano and rumoca about 10 s per model; one 24-hour plan 5 to 20 s; one two-day closed loop with moving horizon estimation about ten minutes; the rule-based reference a second.

docs.title: 1. From the YAML to the CasADi model¶
docs.text: tutorials/buildings/house/base.yaml describes a 100 m2 house: cavity walls, triple glazing, a concrete slab, a 3.5 kW air-to-water heat pump with a 150 l buffer tank, a mixing valve and a low-temperature radiator behind a thermostatic valve. Trano renders it with its FastModelMPC library (physics close to the Buildings library: layered walls, window optics, water nodes) where the controls of the systems are inputs, and with its FastModel library where the controllers of the YAML close the loop (the rule-based reference). rumoca translates each into an explicit CasADi ODE xdot = f(t, x, u, d, p).

docs.title: 2. One economic MPC plan¶
docs.text: The controller minimises, over the horizon, the electricity bought (read from the meter of the heat pump) at the tariff price, plus penalties on the comfort band, subject to the ODE collocated on Radau points and the bounds of the controls; IPOPT solves the nonlinear programme. With a flat price it heats just enough and as late as the slow radiator allows; with a time-varying price it charges the buffer, the water and the walls when electricity is cheap. Try it: the widget re-solves the plan (5 to 20 s; the next solves warm start from the previous plan).

docs.title: 3. Closed loop against the true building¶
docs.text: A plan is not a result: the controller applies the first step, the building responds, the sensor reports the air temperature, the state is estimated and the plan is rebuilt. The true building has its envelope conductances and capacities, air capacity and infiltration drawn at random (20 %) and a sensor noise of 0.1 K; the controller keeps the Trano model. The runs are cached; Recompute runs one again (about ten minutes).

docs.title: MPC against the controllers of the YAML¶
docs.text: The same building, period, tariff and comfort band, controlled by the thermostat, heating curve and buffer controller written in the YAML (the closed-loop FastModel, simulated in a second): this is the reference an MPC has to beat.

docs.title: The price of not knowing the building¶
docs.text: The same price and band with the plant equal to the control model (and its true state) and with the true building: the cost difference is the price of the model error, the comfort violations show where the controller was over-confident.

docs.title: 4. Why state estimation matters¶
docs.text: The controller needs the full state: the wall layers, the water of the radiator and the buffer. It measures the air temperature only. The moving horizon estimator fits the trajectory of the model to the measurements of the last hours; below, its estimate of the buffer and of the inner layer of a wall against the true building, then three runs on the same true building: the true state handed to the controller, moving horizon estimation, and no estimation (the measured air temperature, the other states held at their expected start values).

docs.title: Key takeaways¶
docs.text:
• The MPC beats the controllers of the YAML on both counts: over the same two January days, on the true building, it costs 5 to 8 % less (3.21 against 3.48 EUR under day-ahead prices for the base house, 6.46 against 6.87 EUR for the old one) with 1.4 K.h of comfort violation against 48 K.h for the thermostat, which hovers at the bottom of the band; it uses about 5 % less energy because the house is never overheated.
  • The price signal moves the heating, not the bill: under day-ahead prices the MPC buys 58 % of its energy in the cheap third of the hours (40 % for the thermostat, by chance of the night setback); with so flat a winter price profile the saving is a few cents, the flexibility is what the next tutorial sells.
  • Model error costs about 5 %: against the true building (envelope 20 % off, noisy sensor) the same controller pays 3.17 instead of 3.02 EUR and lets the air drift 1.5 K.h outside the band; with the model as the plant the violation is nil.
  • State estimation is not optional: with the air temperature only (the other states held at their expected values) the controller under-heats, saves 17 % and violates the band by 41 K.h with 2.3 K at worst; the moving horizon estimate (1.4 K.h) even beats the true state handed over (2.3 K.h), because its bias absorbs part of the model error.

docs.title: Further reading¶
docs.text:
• tutorials/references.md, section A: Drgoňa et al. (2020) for MPC in buildings, Blum et al. (2021) for the KPIs used here.
  • docs/mpc.md for the optimisation problem and docs/estimation.md for the estimator.
  • Next: 02_flexibility_use_cases quantifies what this flexibility is worth under real price signals, capacity tariffs and explicit activation requests.

docs.title: 02 - Flexibility use cases: what the house can do for the grid, and what it costs¶
docs.text:
Learning objectives

  1. Quantify implicit flexibility: what the price-aware controller saves against a price-agnostic one under day-ahead prices, how much energy it moves in time, and what planning on the 15-minute market time unit changes.
  2. Shave the peak under a capacity tariff on the monthly peak (the Flemish capaciteitstarief): how the controller trades energy cost against capacity cost, and why the floor of the tariff matters for a small heat pump.
  3. Deliver explicit flexibility: respond to an up or down activation request against a baseline, measure the delivered energy and the rebound.
  4. Map the flexibility envelope (power versus duration, at what cost) and the response to a price step (the flexibility function).
  5. See what negative prices do to a house with PV.

The definitions follow IEA EBC Annex 67 and the characterisation of Reynders, Diriken and Saelens (2017), the flexibility function of Junker et al. (2018) and the BOPTEST KPIs of Blum et al. (2021); every source is listed in tutorials/references.md. The closed loops (against the true building of tutorial 01, with moving horizon estimation) come from tutorials/cache/flexibility/ (make cache); the plans of section 1 are solved live.

Runtimes (this container): a two-day hourly closed loop about ten minutes; a 24-hour plan 5 to 20 s at hourly steps, one to two minutes at 15-minute steps; the envelope about twenty plans.

docs.title: 1. Implicit flexibility under day-ahead prices¶
docs.text: The price-agnostic controller has the same model, comfort band and constraints, but plans at the mean price of the period; costing its run with the day-ahead tariff gives what the house would pay without reacting to the price. The difference is what the flexibility is worth under that tariff (value_of_flexibility).

docs.title: Hourly or 15-minute planning¶
docs.text: Since 1 October 2025 the single day-ahead coupling trades 15-minute products. Below, the same plan at hourly and at 15-minute steps (the same 24-hour horizon: 24 or 96 steps, four times the variables). A heat pump on a buffer can follow a quarter-hour price only through its compressor: compare the energy bought and the cost.

docs.title: 2. Peak shaving under the capacity tariff¶
docs.text: The Flemish distribution tariff bills the average of the twelve monthly peaks (highest quarter-hour average power of the month, floored at 2.5 kW) at about 50 EUR/kW/year (2025 levels: 48.9 to 56.9 depending on the area). One extra kilowatt of monthly peak costs about 4 EUR; the controller carries the peak of the month so far and weighs the energy saving of a cheap-hour boost against the capacity cost of a higher peak. The runs use a time-of-use tariff and a deep night setback (5 K), so that the morning recovery makes the peak. With hourly steps the peak is the hourly average, which underestimates the quarter-hour peak.

docs.title: 3. Explicit flexibility: activation requests and the rebound¶
docs.text: An aggregator or the DSO asks for a change of the electricity bought during a window against a baseline (here the run of the same controller without the request). The controller receives the request as a soft cap (down) or floor (up) one hour before the window (ActivationRequest.notice_hours), delivers what the comfort band allows and rebounds afterwards: the heat not delivered during a shed is delivered later, the heat stored during an upward activation is not bought later. The metrics give the delivered energy, the rebound energy and peak and their ratio, in the spirit of the available storage capacity and storage efficiency of Reynders et al.

docs.title: 4. Flexibility envelope and flexibility function¶
docs.text: The envelope answers the aggregator's question before any request: from the current state, how much power can the house shed or absorb for one, two or four hours without leaving the comfort band, and what does that plan cost against the unconstrained one? It is a sweep of constrained MPC plans (bisection on the cap or floor of the electricity bought; absorbing is bounded by the full-load power of the heat pump).

docs.title: 5. Negative prices and PV¶
docs.text: With 20 m2 of PV the house exports at midday; a negative wholesale price (a renewable surplus) turns the midday import into something the controller wants: it charges the buffer and the walls, and the export is paid at the (negative) export price. Self-consumption is the share of the generation used on site.

docs.title: Key takeaways¶
docs.text:
• Implicit flexibility is worth little with a flat winter price: the price-aware controller shifts 0.8 kWh (base house) to 3.2 kWh (old house) into the cheap hours over two days and saves 0.45 % of the bill. The synthetic day-ahead signal has a small spread in January; the saving scales with the spread, not with the building (tutorials/scripts/fetch_prices.py brings a real year in). The 15-minute plan costs twenty times the solve for a 3 % different answer: the hour is the right step for a heavy house.
  • A capacity tariff is the strong signal: at 150 EUR/kW/year without a floor the base house cuts its monthly peak by 81 % (1.77 to 0.34 kW) and the old house by 78 %, trading a little comfort (1.6 against 1.0 K.h); with a 2.5 kW floor the base house has nothing to gain (its peak is below the floor) and pays the floor.
  • Explicit activations are delivered when the plan has room: a 1 kW absorption at 13h is delivered in full with a 0.6 kWh rebound over the next three hours; a 0.3 kW shed at 17h is delivered at 83 % over two hours and 57 % over four, because the evening plan is already lean. The envelope says the same: at 13h and 19h the house can absorb 1.3 to 1.5 kW for hours, it can shed almost nothing.
  • PV without a battery does not react to negative prices: with 9.3 kWh of January PV consumed on site and nothing to charge, the controller's day costs the same (1.53 EUR) whether midday prices go negative or not; tutorial 05 adds the storages that make them count.

docs.title: Further reading¶
docs.text: tutorials/references.md: Annex 67 and Annex 82 for the definitions, Reynders, Diriken and Saelens (2017) and Stinner et al. (2016) for the characterisation, Junker et al. (2018) for the flexibility function, the Vlaamse Nutsregulator sheets for the capacity tariff.

docs.title: 03 - Calibration: the YAML declares the parameters, IPOPT finds them¶
docs.text:
Learning objectives

  1. Declare the parameters to calibrate in the Trano YAML itself ({value, parameter: true, min, max}), keep it the single source of truth, and see which parameters of the CasADi model each field moves.
  2. Calibrate the closed-loop model (the controllers of the YAML inside, no control input) on monitoring data a real building would give: a noisy air temperature and an electricity meter, no valve positions.
  3. Read how IPOPT solves it: the three fields as decision variables, the closed-loop model simulated with CVODES inside a weighted least squares with priors, the gradient from the adjoint sensitivities of the integrator.
  4. Compare the model before and after: the temperatures and the energy on the training days and on two validation days, and the recovered values against the true ones.

The true building, its data and the calibration come from tutorials/cache/calibration/ (make cache); the calibration is solved live when the notebook does not run in quick mode (a few minutes).

Runtimes (this container): one regeneration of the model by Trano and rumoca about 15 s (one per declared parameter, for the sensitivities); the calibration of three days of hourly data, 38 states, two to five minutes.

docs.title: 1. The parameters, declared in the YAML¶
docs.text: tests/models/single_zone_calibration.yaml is the heat pump house of tutorial 01 with its cavity wall spelled out and three fields annotated: the conductivity of the insulation, its thickness and the infiltration rate. CalibrationSpec reads them by path (the convention of trano.runtime) and writes the flat copy Trano reads.

docs.title: 2. The true building and its monitoring data¶
docs.text: The true building is the same YAML with other values of the three parameters: a worse insulation, thinner than drawn, and a leakier house. It is run by its own controllers (the closed-loop FastModel: thermostat, heating curve, buffer control) over five cold days of January, after two days of spin-up; the monitoring system records the weather, the air temperature with 0.1 K of noise and the electricity meter with 20 Wh of noise. It does not record the valves or the compressor: the model being calibrated has its controllers inside.

docs.title: 3. Before: the model with the values of the YAML¶
docs.text: An open-loop simulation of the model from the first measurement, with the assumed parameters: the house loses less heat than the true one, so it stays warmer and draws less electricity.

docs.title: 4. How IPOPT calibrates it¶
docs.text:
The calibration is one nonlinear programme over the whole training period, solved by single shooting (CalibrationSettings.method, chosen automatically for a closed-loop model):

  • decision variables: one per declared parameter, log(field / value), bounded by log(min / value) and log(max / value); nothing else. The parameters of the model are expressions of the fields (p = p0 * (field / value) ** e, the exponents measured above; a conductivity and a thickness both move the conductance of the insulation layer, their factors compound).
  • the simulation inside the objective: CVODES integrates the closed-loop model hour by hour, with the parameters of the candidate, from the start values of the Modelica model through two days of spin-up before the data (so that the walls, the water and the controller states at the start are those of the candidate, not of the nominal model) and then over the training days with their weather.
  • the gradient: central differences of the objective with a step of 5 % of a field, 2n + 1 simulations of a second each; IPOPT's Hessian is a quasi-Newton (L-BFGS) one and it takes its full steps. A thermostat that flips one integration step earlier makes the objective jumpy at the scale of a tenth of a percent of a field: the adjoint sensitivities of the integrator and small finite differences read that noise and stall IPOPT short of the optimum, a wide step reads the slope of the valley through it and a sufficient-decrease test would refuse steps for the same jumps.
  • objective: the squared errors of the simulated air temperature against the measurements (weighted by the sensor noise), of the energy metered over each hour against the meter (weighted by the meter noise), and the squared deviations of the fields from their prior (the YAML).

The models with control inputs (the MPC models of the other tutorials) are calibrated on their Radau collocation instead, the states as decision variables and the dynamics as constraints: well conditioned over long periods and poor initial parameters. Not here: the thermostat, the hysteresis of the heat pump controller and the valve limits make the collocated dynamics of a closed-loop model non-smooth, and IPOPT crawls for hundreds of iterations without converging; a simulation follows these switches in under a second, and three parameters need a handful of iterations. The log below is IPOPT's own (one line per iteration: the objective, the dual infeasibility, the step).

docs.title: 5. After: the fit on the training and validation days, and what the two fields became¶
6. Identifiability: what the data can and cannot tell apart¶
docs.text:
The calibrated model reproduces the air temperature and the electricity of the true building on days it has not seen, but the two fields did not land on their true values: a leakier house and a worse insulation are both a loss proportional to the indoor-outdoor temperature difference. The data of a thermostat-controlled house fix the total loss; how it splits between the walls and the infiltration is a flat valley of the objective, and the prior (the YAML) and the first steps of IPOPT decide where along it the fit stops.

What a measurement can add: a blower-door test gives the infiltration rate. With the YAML regenerated at that rate and the conductivity as the only declared parameter, the same fit recovers it.

docs.title: Key takeaways¶
docs.text:
• The YAML is the specification of the calibration too: three fields carry {value, parameter: true, min, max}, CalibrationSpec writes the flat copy Trano reads and measures which parameters of the CasADi model each field moves; the fit adjusts the fields within their bounds and the model follows.
  • A closed-loop model is calibrated by simulation, not collocation: its thermostat and hysteresis make the collocated problem non-smooth; the single-shooting fit (two decision variables, CVODES inside the objective, wide central differences) brings the air-temperature error from 1.35 K to 0.18 K on the training days and from 1.14 K to 0.15 K on two unseen days, with the energy use to match.
  • The data decide what is identifiable: the free fit lands at a conductivity of 0.052 and 0.63 air changes per hour (true: 0.060 and 0.60) - the right total loss, split along a flat valley the objective barely feels; with the infiltration measured, the conductivity comes out at 0.0593. Declare in the YAML what a measurement cannot give, fix the rest.
  • The remaining 0.17 K is the switching: a thermostat that flips one integration step earlier moves the hourly sample; the fitted model has the right parameters but not the exact switching times, which is what IPOPT's jumpy log in section 4 shows.

docs.title: Further reading¶
docs.text:
• docs/calibration.md for the groups and the problem; mpctrano.yaml_parameters for the annotations.
  • Trano's runtime package addresses the same YAML fields by path for the Buildings models compiled with OpenModelica (trano.runtime.specification): the two conventions agree.

docs.title: 04 - An office in summer: cooling, occupancy and the price of comfort¶
docs.text:
Learning objectives

  1. Model cooling with Trano's FastModel: the ideal emitter of a zone is a heat flow the controller decides; letting it go negative turns it into a chiller, costed at an EER.
  2. Read a cooling plan: the sun and the occupants drive the load, the mass of the building and the price signal decide when the chiller runs (pre-cooling at night under day-ahead prices).
  3. Weigh comfort against cost: the office without cooling (the controllers of the YAML in summer) against the MPC, and the peak of the chiller under a capacity charge.

The closed loops come from tutorials/cache/office/ (uv run python tutorials/scripts/build_cache.py office); the plans are solved live.

Runtimes (hourly steps, this container): Trano and rumoca about 15 s; one 24-hour plan of this two-zone office one to two minutes (52 states, two heat flows); one closed-loop day about an hour.

docs.title: 1. The office and its emitters¶
docs.text: tutorials/buildings/office/base.yaml: an open-plan office of 200 m2 with 36 m2 of south glazing and a meeting area of 80 m2, externally insulated walls, a flat roof, occupied from 8h to 18h (12 W/m2 of occupants and equipment in the open plan). Each zone has an ideal emitter (radiator of variant ideal in the YAML): in the FastModelMPC model it is an input Q_flow [W], which Trano bounds to heating (min=0). The study lets it go negative (FastModel.with_control_bounds): the same equations cool the zone. The electricity follows from a COP of 3.5 for heating and an EER of 3 for cooling (MPCSettings.heat_cop, cooling_eer).

docs.title: 2. A summer day: flat price against day-ahead prices¶
docs.text: The comfort band is 21 to 25 degC when occupied, free floating between 15 and 30 degC otherwise. With a flat price the controller cools as late as possible; with day-ahead prices it may pre-cool the mass at night, when electricity is cheap, if the saving beats the extra losses.

docs.title: 3. The closed loop: the MPC against no cooling¶
docs.text: The true office (perturbed envelope, noisy sensors) over one working day with moving horizon estimation, against the office without cooling: the closed-loop model of the YAML has the thermostats of the heating only, so in summer it free floats. Its "cost" is the comfort it loses.

docs.title: 4. The peak of the chiller under a capacity charge¶
docs.text: A capacity charge on the peak of the day (here 8 EUR/kW, the monthly charge of the Flemish capacity tariff at about 100 EUR/kW/year) makes the controller spread the cooling: lower peak, more kWh.

docs.title: Key takeaways¶
docs.text:
• Cooling is the same optimisation with the sign flipped: the ideal emitters of the YAML, their lower bound made negative, cool the two zones at a fixed EER; on the hottest day of the year the office needs 37 kWh of cooling, 12.4 kWh of electricity and a 1.8 kW peak, and keeps the band to 0.7 K.h where the office without cooling exceeds it by 52 K.h and 5.4 K at worst.
  • Day-ahead prices move nothing here: the plan under day-ahead prices is the plan under a flat price (3.17 against 3.15 EUR). Summer prices are flat where the cooling load is, the night is already cool and cooling the mass in advance costs the same electricity: there is no price spread to arbitrage with a constant EER.
  • A capacity charge is what moves the chiller: at 8 EUR/kW of monthly peak the controller pre-cools the slab and the walls through the night, shaves the peak from 1.80 to 1.40 kW and pays for it with 75 % more electricity (21.7 against 12.4 kWh); the bill still falls, by less than a euro over the day, because the capacity charge is the larger term. Whether the pre-cooling is worth it depends on that charge: see tutorials/references.md on capacity tariffs.

docs.title: Further reading¶
docs.text:
• tutorials/references.md: the characterisation of flexibility (Reynders et al.) applies to cooling as to heating; Blum et al. (2021) for the KPIs.
  • The chiller is a constant EER here; a chiller and a cooling coil in the FastModel library of Trano would give the part-load behaviour (see tutorials/PLAN.md).

docs.title: 05 - PV, a battery and an electric vehicle next to the thermal storage¶
docs.text:
Learning objectives

  1. Put electrical storages next to the thermal one: a stationary battery and a vehicle charged at home are optimised in the balance of the meter, with the heat pump, the buffer and the walls of the house.
  2. Read the dispatch order under day-ahead prices and under negative midday prices: which storage takes the cheap or free energy first, what is exported, how much of the PV is consumed on site.
  3. See the vehicle's deadline: it leaves at 7h with 30 kWh and comes back at 18h 12 kWh lower; the controller charges it when the night is cheap, not when it arrives.

The storages are linear state-of-charge models in the controller (Battery, ElectricVehicle, MPCSettings.batteries and .vehicles): Trano's FastModel describes the building and its thermal systems, mpctrano the electrical assets at the meter. The closed loops come from tutorials/cache/pv/ (uv run python tutorials/scripts/build_cache.py pv); the plans are solved live.

Runtimes (hourly steps, this container): one 24-hour plan of the PV house 10 to 50 s; one closed-loop day with the storages 10 to 30 minutes.

docs.title: 1. The house with PV, and the storages¶
docs.text: tutorials/buildings/house/pv.yaml is the house of tutorial 01 with 20 m2 of PV on the south roof (about 4 kWp): Trano meters its production (pv_001.EPro), which the controller nets against the heat pump at the meter. The battery (8 kWh, 3 kW, 92 % round trip) and the vehicle (50 kWh, 7.4 kW charger, home from 18h to 7h, 12 kWh a day, 30 kWh required at departure) are declared in the controller settings.

docs.title: 2. One plan: the dispatch under day-ahead prices¶
docs.text: The plan below runs the house, the battery and the vehicle together over a January day. Look at where the battery charges (the cheap night, the midday PV) and discharges (the evening peak), and at the vehicle: charged in the cheap hours before 7h, idle while away, charged again after 18h only if the night is not cheaper.

docs.title: 3. Negative prices at midday¶
docs.text: A negative wholesale price (a renewable surplus) makes importing worth money: the controller charges everything that can take it, the battery, the vehicle if it is home (it is not, at midday on a weekday), the buffer and the walls, and stops exporting the PV. Compare the two plans on the storages:

docs.title: 4. The closed loop: with and without the storages¶
docs.text: One day against the true building (perturbed envelope, noisy sensors) with moving horizon estimation, for the house alone, with the battery, and with the battery and the vehicle, under the two price signals; the controllers of the YAML (no storage, the PV exports what the house does not use) as the reference. The vehicle's driving energy is bought in every run that has it: compare the cost per kWh rather than the total.

docs.title: Key takeaways¶
docs.text:
• The storages sit in one balance: the heat pump, the buffer and the walls (through the FastModel), the battery and the vehicle (exact linear models in the controller) share the meter; the controller dispatches them together against the same price. In January the 20 m2 of PV give 5 kWh a day, and the MPC consumes all of it on site (self-consumption 1.00) where the controllers of the YAML export more than half (2.7 kWh sold, 0.46).
  • The battery earns little under day-ahead prices and more under negative ones: 0.70 to 0.66 EUR a day with the winter spread of the day-ahead signal; 0.70 to 0.50 EUR when the midday prices go negative, because the battery is paid to charge (7.5 kWh charged, 4.3 kWh bought for a house that needs 2.9).
  • The vehicle is a deadline, not a storage: the 12 kWh it needs by 7h are charged in the cheapest night hours (5.2 kWh over the day from a half-full battery); its 7.4 kW charger sets the peak of the house (8.4 kW under day-ahead prices, 4.9 kW when the negative midday hours spread the charging) - the capacity tariff of tutorial 02 is what would tame it.

docs.title: Further reading¶
docs.text:
• tutorials/references.md: Annex 67 for the storage order and the self-consumption indicators.
  • The storages are exact linear models here; a battery and a charger as FastModel components in Trano would put them in the Modelica model with their losses (see tutorials/PLAN.md).

docs.title: 06 - Your building: edit the YAML, plan, and compare with its own controllers¶
docs.text:
Learning objectives

  1. Change the building in the Trano YAML (insulation, windows, heat pump, buffer, set points, schedules) and regenerate the CasADi model in seconds: the whole chain of the tutorials runs from one editable cell.
  2. Plan the heating of your building with the economic MPC and read what the change did to the plan.
  3. Run the closed loop against the controllers written in the YAML (the rule-based reference) and compare the cost, the energy and the comfort of two versions of the building side by side.

Everything is computed live (nothing is cached): Trano and rumoca take 10 to 30 s per building, a plan 5 to 20 s, one day of closed loop two to four minutes (six hours in quick mode).

docs.title: 1. The building, in one cell¶
docs.text:
The YAML below is the house of tutorial 01 (tutorials/buildings/house/base.yaml): a 100 m2 single zone with cavity walls, triple glazing and a concrete slab, heated by a 3.5 kW air-to-water heat pump with a 150 l buffer and a low-temperature radiator. Edit it and run the notebook again. Some things to try:

  • the envelope: the wall and window surfaces, their azimuth (0 is south), the constructions (CAVITYWALL:001 is the insulated cavity wall of Trano's defaults; tutorials/buildings/house/old.yaml shows an uninsulated one with its own material and constructions sections);
  • the systems: nominal_heating_power of the heat pump, tank_volume of the buffer, the supply set point temperature_supply_setpoint_heat_pump, the radiator's nominal_heating_power_positive_for_heating;
  • the controllers of the YAML (the rule-based reference, not the MPC): the thermostat set point, setback and schedule of emission_control, the occupancy schedule and gains.

The weather file of the house (Uccle, typical meteorological year) is copied next to the YAML. The names of the elements (SPACE:001, BOILER:001...) are the names of the variables of the model; keep them, or read the new ones from model.state_names.

docs.title: 2. Plan its heating¶
docs.text: The widget re-solves one open-loop plan of your building from the state its own controllers reach after the spin-up (prices, comfort band, horizon, comfort weight); the static plan below it is the one the notebook renders without a kernel.

docs.title: 3. Closed loop: the MPC against the controllers of the YAML¶
docs.text: One day of closed loop (the model is the building here: no mismatch, the true state is handed to the controller, so that the run takes minutes), and the same day with the thermostat, heating curve and buffer controller of the YAML, costed with the same tariff and assessed against the same band. The band is the one of tutorial 01 (21 to 24 degC when occupied, a 3 K setback at night).

docs.title: 4. Two versions side by side¶
docs.text: A second version of the building, from the same text with one change (here a 300 l buffer instead of 150 l: twice the fast storage the MPC charges in the cheap hours), run through the same comparison. Replace the replace with your own change, or with a second YAML.

docs.title: Key takeaways¶
docs.text:
• The YAML is the only input: one cell rewrites the building, Trano and rumoca regenerate the MPC model and the rule-based reference, and the rest of the tutorials (plan widget, closed loop, KPIs) applies unchanged.
  • The comparison with the controllers of the YAML is the fair one: same building, same weather, same tariff, same comfort band, same spun-up state; what the MPC gains comes from timing the heat pump on the price and from using the buffer and the walls as storage.
  • A larger buffer helps the MPC and hurts the thermostat (as written: the MPC's day falls from 1.41 to 1.38 EUR with two thirds of the energy bought in the cheap hours, the thermostat's rises from 1.53 to 1.64 EUR): the reference charges the buffer to its set point whatever the price and loses more from a bigger tank, the MPC charges it when electricity is cheap and only as much as the house will need.
